content: Typhoid fever is a severe illness caused by the bacterium Salmonella Typhi. It can lead to high fever, weakness, abdominal pain, headache, loss of appetite, and sometimes a rash. If left untreated, it can be fatal in up to 30% of cases. Some individuals who recover from typhoid may become carriers, capable of spreading the disease to others. The primary mode of transmission is through contaminated food or water. In the United States, most cases occur in individuals who have traveled to regions where typhoid is prevalent. Globally, typhoid affects approximately 21 million people annually and causes around 200,000 deaths. Vaccination against typhoid can help prevent the disease. There are two types of typhoid vaccines available: 1. Inactivated (killed) vaccine, which is administered as an injection. 2. Live, attenuated (weakened) vaccine, which is taken orally. Routine typhoid vaccination is not recommended in the United States. However, it is advised for: Travelers to areas where typhoid is common. (Note: The vaccine is not 100% effective and does not replace the need for caution regarding food and water consumption.) Individuals in close contact with a typhoid carrier. Laboratory workers who handle Salmonella Typhi bacteria. Inactivated Typhoid Vaccine (Injection): Not recommended for children under 2 years of age. A single dose provides protection and should be administered at least 2 weeks before travel to allow the vaccine to take effect. A booster dose is required every 2 years for individuals who remain at risk. Live Typhoid Vaccine (Oral): Not recommended for children under 6 years of age. Requires four doses, taken two days apart. The final dose should be completed at least 1 week before travel to ensure effectiveness. A booster dose is needed every 5 years for individuals who remain at risk. This vaccine should not be taken within 24 hours of certain antibiotics. Both vaccines can be administered alongside other vaccines. Who Should Not Receive the Typhoid Vaccine or Should Delay Vaccination: Inactivated Typhoid Vaccine (Injection): Individuals who have had a severe reaction to a previous dose of this vaccine should not receive it again. Live Typhoid Vaccine (Oral): Individuals who have had a severe reaction to a previous dose of this vaccine should not receive it again. Those with weakened immune systems should avoid this vaccine and opt for the inactivated version instead. This includes individuals with: HIV/AIDS or other immune-compromising conditions. Those undergoing treatment with immune-suppressing drugs (e.g., steroids for 2 weeks or longer). Cancer patients or those receiving cancer treatments such as radiation or chemotherapy. Side Effects: Like any medication, vaccines can potentially cause serious problems, such as severe allergic reactions. However, the risk of a vaccine causing significant harm or death is extremely low. Serious complications from either typhoid vaccine are very rare. Mild Side Effects (Inactivated Typhoid Vaccine): Fever (occurs in about 1 in 100 people). Headache (occurs in about 3 in 100 people). Redness or swelling at the injection site (occurs in about 7 in 100 people). Mild Side Effects (Live Typhoid Vaccine): Fever or headache (occurs in about 5 in 100 people). Abdominal discomfort, nausea, vomiting, or rash (rare). What to Do in Case of a Moderate or Severe Reaction: Look for unusual symptoms, such as high fever or behavioral changes. Signs of a severe allergic reaction may include difficulty breathing, hoarseness or wheezing, hives, paleness, weakness, rapid heartbeat, or dizziness. If any of these symptoms occur, seek medical attention immediately. Inform the healthcare provider about the reaction, including the date and time it occurred and when the vaccine was administered. Ask the healthcare provider to file a Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) form. Alternatively, you can contact VAERS directly at 1-800-822-7967 or visit their website. National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program: In the rare event of a serious reaction to a vaccine, a federal program exists to help cover the costs of care for those affected. For more information, call 1-800-338-2382 or visit the program's website. How to Learn More: Consult your doctor or healthcare provider. They can provide the vaccine package insert or recommend additional resources. Contact your local or state health department's immunization program. Reach out to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) by calling 1-800-232-4636 (1-800-CDC-INFO) or visiting the National Immunization Program's website.
